reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly identifies trade-off or opportunity cost on diagnostic questions Q1 or Q7.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students confuse trade-off (the set of all alternatives) with opportunity cost (the value of the next-best alternative foregone).

miniLesson.explain: A trade-off is the full range of alternative options you have when making a decision. For example, if you have $20 and can buy a book, go to a movie, or save the money, all three possibilities are part of your trade-off. Opportunity cost is specifically the value of the next-best alternative that you give up. If you choose the book, the opportunity cost is the enjoyment of the movie (your second-best option), not the act of saving. Opportunity cost is always the next-best alternative, not all alternatives, and it is determined at the moment of decision.
miniLesson.example: Consider a student deciding between studying for a test and going to a party. The trade-off includes studying, partying, and possibly other activities. If the student chooses to study, the opportunity cost is the fun and social time at the party (the next-best alternative). The trade-off is the whole set of options; the opportunity cost is just the value of the one foregone.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Trade-off is the buffet of options; opportunity cost is the one dish you leave behind.

guidedPractice.prompt: Your family has $50 to spend on either dinner out or a board game. List two items in the trade-off and state the opportunity cost if you choose dinner out.
guidedPractice.answer: Trade-off includes dinner out and board game (and maybe other options). Opportunity cost of dinner out is the board game (value of next-best alternative).

guidedPractice.prompt: A government must choose between funding a new park or a new library. Identify the trade-off and the opportunity cost of choosing the library.
guidedPractice.answer: The trade-off includes the park and the library (and possibly other projects). The opportunity cost of the library is the value of the park (the next-best alternative).

guidedPractice.prompt: Maria has a free evening. She can watch a movie, exercise, or work on a hobby. She chooses to exercise. Explain the difference between her trade-off and the opportunity cost. What is the opportunity cost if her second choice was watching a movie?
guidedPractice.answer: The trade-off is all three options (movie, exercise, hobby). The opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative, which is watching the movie (since that was her second choice). This is distinct from the other alternatives in the trade-off.

reteachModules.trigger: Student picks wrong option on Q2 or Q5 of the diagnostic test.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student thinks opportunity cost is the same as future consequences, failing to recognize that opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative at the time of decision, while consequences are outcomes that occur later.

miniLesson.explain: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative you give up when making a decision, and it occurs at the moment of choice. Consequences, on the other hand, are the future results of your decision. They are not the same. For example, if you choose to study instead of going to a party, the opportunity cost is the enjoyment and social time you forego (the value of the party). The consequence could be a good grade on the exam. The grade is not the opportunity cost; it is a future outcome.
miniLesson.example: Consider a student who sacrifices social time for health improvement (from the lesson). If they choose to exercise instead of hanging out with friends, the opportunity cost is the fun and connection with friends. The consequence might be better physical health. The two are distinct.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Opportunity cost = what you give up AT DECISION TIME. Consequences = what happens LATER.

guidedPractice.prompt: Suppose you have $20 and must choose between buying a new book or going to a movie. You choose the book. Which of the following is the opportunity cost? A) The enjoyment from the movie you gave up. B) The price of the movie ticket. C) The knowledge you will gain from the book. D) The regret of not watching the movie.
guidedPractice.answer: A) The enjoyment from the movie you gave up. (This is the value of the next-best alternative at decision time.)

guidedPractice.prompt: You have two hours of free time and can either study for a test or play video games. You choose to study. Identify the opportunity cost of your decision and explain why the test score you receive later is NOT part of the opportunity cost.
guidedPractice.answer: The opportunity cost is the enjoyment and relaxation you would have had from playing video games. The test score is a consequence of your decision, not the opportunity cost, because opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative foregone at the time of decision, while consequences are future outcomes.

guidedPractice.prompt: A city council has a limited budget and must choose between building a new park or a new community center. They decide to build the park. Some citizens argue that the opportunity cost is the future benefits of the community center that will be lost. Are they correct? Explain why or why not, using the distinction between opportunity cost and consequences.
guidedPractice.answer: They are not correct. The opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative foregone, which is the community center itself (the foregone alternative). The future benefits of the community center are consequences of not building it, not the opportunity cost. Opportunity cost is incurred at the moment of decision and is the value of the alternative given up, not the future outcomes of the chosen action.

reteachModules.trigger: Student answers incorrectly on questions about why trade-offs exist or the necessity of cost-benefit analysis due to scarcity.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may overlook that scarcity underlies all trade-offs and cost-benefit analysis, leading to decisions without considering resource limits.

miniLesson.explain: Scarcity means that resources are limited while our wants are unlimited. Because of scarcity, we cannot have everything we want, so we must make choices. Every choice involves a trade-off (all the alternatives we give up) and an opportunity cost (the value of the next-best alternative). Scarcity is the fundamental reason why trade-offs and cost-benefit analysis are necessary in economics. Without scarcity, there would be no need to choose.
miniLesson.example: Students shared personal trade-offs: giving up entertainment for academic progress, and sacrificing social time for health improvement. These choices exist because time and energy are scarce. Similarly, Group 2 affirmed that cost-benefit assessment avoids irrational decisions and minimizes resource loss. The scarcity of time and money forced them to evaluate their options.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: 'Scarcity is the mother of all trade-offs.' Without scarcity, we would never have to choose.

guidedPractice.prompt: Why do we face trade-offs in economic decisions? Choose the correct answer. A) Because people have unlimited wants, but resources are scarce. B) Because governments set rules that limit our choices. C) Because we always want to maximize profit. D) Because technology is not advanced enough.
guidedPractice.answer: A) Because people have unlimited wants, but resources are scarce.

guidedPractice.prompt: Because resources are scarce, which of the following is most important when making a major economic decision? A) Follow the majority opinion. B) Choose the option that has the lowest immediate cost. C) Weigh the expected costs and benefits to maximize net benefit. D) Avoid making any decision until more resources appear.
guidedPractice.answer: C) Weigh the expected costs and benefits to maximize net benefit.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student argues that 'since we have to make trade-offs anyway, scarcity doesn't really affect our decisions.' Explain why this statement is incorrect, using the concept of scarcity and the need for cost-benefit analysis.
guidedPractice.answer: The statement is incorrect because scarcity is the very reason trade-offs exist. Without scarcity (unlimited resources), we could satisfy all wants and never need to choose. Scarcity forces us to prioritize and evaluate alternatives. Cost-benefit analysis is necessary precisely because resources are limited; it helps us allocate scarce resources to options that yield the highest net benefit. Ignoring scarcity would lead to irrational decisions that waste resources.

reteachModules.trigger: Student picks wrong option on Q4 (evaluate government spending decision).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may assume governments should always minimize costs; the lesson emphasized balanced investment for long-term benefits.

miniLesson.explain: When making decisions about public services, governments should not always choose the lowest-cost option. A balanced investment in areas like healthcare and transportation supports long-term economic stability. Cost-benefit analysis helps evaluate both immediate costs and future benefits.
miniLesson.example: Group 1 from the lesson concluded that governments should not solely pursue cost reduction in public services (e.g., medical, transport) to ensure long-term sustainability. For instance, spending more on a transit system now may reduce traffic and pollution later.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think 'balance, not bottom line' – lowest cost today can mean higher costs tomorrow.

guidedPractice.prompt: True or False: Governments should always pick the cheapest option for public services.
guidedPractice.answer: False. Governments should consider long-term benefits, not just low costs.

guidedPractice.prompt: Explain why a city might choose to invest in a more expensive public transit system rather than a cheaper one.
guidedPractice.answer: Because the more expensive system may provide greater long-term benefits such as reduced traffic congestion, lower pollution, and economic growth, which a cost-benefit analysis would show outweigh the initial cost.

guidedPractice.prompt: A government faces a limited budget and must decide between funding a new hospital or a road repair project. The hospital costs more but will save lives; the road repair is cheaper but prevents accidents. Describe how cost-benefit analysis should be used to make this decision, and explain why choosing the cheaper option is not always best.
guidedPractice.answer: Cost-benefit analysis should weigh all expected costs and benefits over time, including non-monetary ones like lives saved and safety. The cheaper option (road repair) might have lower immediate cost but could miss significant health benefits. Choosing the cheaper option is not always best because the net benefit of the hospital might be higher despite its cost. Balanced investment in public services supports long-term stability.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between trade-off and opportunity cost?
options: Trade-off includes all alternatives; opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative foregone.
Trade-off and opportunity cost are two terms for the same concept.
Opportunity cost includes all alternatives; trade-off is the value of the next-best alternative.
Trade-off is the cost of a decision; opportunity cost is the benefit of the chosen option.

questions.stem: A city has $1 million to spend. It could build a new park, renovate a library, or upgrade road infrastructure. The city chooses to upgrade roads. Identify the trade-off and the opportunity cost in this decision, and explain why they are different.
questions.rubric: Student correctly identifies trade-off as the set of all three options (park, library, roads) and opportunity cost as the value of the next-best alternative (likely the library or park, whichever is second-best). Student explains that trade-off is the full range of alternatives, while opportunity cost is specifically the value of the one foregone alternative that was next best. Accept any reasonable identification of next-best, as long as student distinguishes the concepts.

questions.stem: A city council is deciding whether to build a new park or a new library, but their budget is limited. Explain how the concept of scarcity influences this decision and why a cost-benefit analysis is necessary.
questions.rubric: Student must mention that scarcity (limited budget) forces a choice; cost-benefit analysis helps compare the benefits and costs of each option to allocate the scarce funds to the project with the highest net benefit to the community.

questions.stem: A city council decides to invest in a more expensive public transit system (light rail) instead of a cheaper bus system. Which of the following is the most likely reason for this decision?
options: The council wants to minimize immediate costs.
The council believes light rail will provide greater long-term benefits despite higher upfront cost.
The council made a mistake and chose the wrong option.
The council ignored cost-benefit analysis.

questions.stem: Explain why a government should not always choose the cheapest option for public services. In your answer, refer to the concept of cost-benefit analysis and the idea of balanced investment for long-term stability.
questions.rubric: Student must: (1) state that governments should consider both costs and benefits, not just costs; (2) explain that cost-benefit analysis weighs long-term benefits against upfront costs; (3) mention that the cheapest option may have lower future benefits or higher long-term costs; (4) imply that balanced investment supports economic stability and public welfare. Accept any reasonable phrasing that captures these ideas.

[err-government-cost-only] student picks wrong option on Q4: Governments should balance costs with long-term benefits, not just minimize spending.

cards.question: What is a 'trade-off' in economics?
options: The value of the best alternative you give up.
All the possible alternatives you face when making a choice.
The future consequences of a decision.
The cost of producing a good.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student distinguishes trade-off from opportunity cost.
misconceptions: That's the definition of opportunity cost, not trade-off.
✓ Correct! A trade-off is the full set of alternatives.
Future consequences are different from trade-offs, which are the alternatives available at decision time.
That is a production cost, not a trade-off.
cards.successCriteria: Student can identify trade-off as the set of all alternatives, not just the next best forgone.
cards.ossdExpectation: Explain how the concepts of scarcity and opportunity costs influence economic decisions, at both the personal and societal levels.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think trade-off means the same as opportunity cost.

cards.question: A student decides to study for an exam instead of going to a party. Which of the following is the opportunity cost of this decision?
options: Enjoyment and social time at the party.
Maybe failing the exam if they had gone to the party.
The time spent studying.
Reduced stress from having studied.
cards.diagnosis: Assess understanding of the temporal distinction between opportunity cost and consequences.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct! The next-best alternative (value of the party) is the opportunity cost.
That's a potential consequence of a different choice, not the opportunity cost of studying.
Time is a resource, but opportunity cost is the value of the forgone alternative, not the resource itself.
That is a benefit of the chosen action, not an opportunity cost.
cards.successCriteria: Student can differentiate between opportunity cost (decision time) and consequences (future outcomes).
cards.ossdExpectation: Explain how the concepts of scarcity and opportunity costs influence economic decisions, at both the personal and societal levels.
cards.commonMisconception: Students equate opportunity cost with later negative outcomes.

cards.question: Why do we face trade-offs in economic decisions?
options: Because people have unlimited wants, but resources are scarce.
Because governments set rules that limit our choices.
Because we always want to maximize profit.
Because technology is not advanced enough.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student understands that scarcity is the root reason for trade-offs.
misconceptions: ✓ Yes! Scarcity of resources relative to unlimited wants forces us to choose among alternatives.
Government rules create constraints, but the fundamental reason is scarcity.
Profit maximization is a goal, not the reason trade-offs exist.
Technology may expand options but does not eliminate scarcity.
cards.successCriteria: Student recognizes that scarcity forces us to make trade-offs.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the significance of the concept of scarcity and how it influences economic choices and decisions of various economic stakeholders.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think trade-offs exist even without scarcity, or that scarcity only applies to money.

cards.question: A city council is deciding whether to invest in a new public transit system. The initial cost is high, but the long-term benefits include reduced traffic and pollution. Which approach best reflects sound economic reasoning?
options: Reject the project because it is too expensive.
Conduct a cost-benefit analysis weighing all costs and benefits over time.
Build a cheaper system even if it is less effective.
Let private companies decide instead of the government.
cards.diagnosis: Assess if student understands that governments should consider long-term benefits, not just minimize costs.
misconceptions: This ignores potential long-term benefits that may outweigh the cost.
✓ Correct! A thorough cost-benefit analysis accounts for both short-term costs and long-term benefits.
Minimizing cost alone may lead to poor long-term outcomes; effectiveness matters too.
Privatization might be considered, but it does not replace the need for evaluating societal costs and benefits.
cards.successCriteria: Student can evaluate government spending decisions beyond cost minimization.
cards.ossdExpectation: Explain the costs and benefits of some individual financial choices.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think governments should always pick the cheapest option.

cards.question: Suppose you have $20 and you must choose between buying a new book or going to a movie. You decide to buy the book. What is the opportunity cost of your decision? Explain in one sentence.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can apply the concept of opportunity cost to a real-life choice.
cards.successCriteria: Student can identify opportunity cost in a scenario and distinguish it from consequences.
cards.ossdExpectation: Explain how the concepts of scarcity and opportunity costs influence economic decisions, at both the personal and societal levels.
cards.commonMisconception: Student lists consequences instead of the value of the next-best alternative.

cards.question: Because resources are scarce, which of the following is most important when making a major economic decision?
options: Follow the majority opinion.
Choose the option that has the lowest immediate cost.
Weigh the expected costs and benefits to maximize net benefit.
Avoid making any decision until more resources appear.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student connects scarcity to the need for systematic evaluation.
misconceptions: Majority opinion does not ensure the best use of scarce resources.
Lowest cost may ignore important benefits; a full evaluation is better.
✓ Yes! Cost-benefit analysis helps allocate scarce resources to options that yield the highest net benefit.
Resources won't appear; decisions must be made with what we have.
cards.successCriteria: Student can explain why cost-benefit analysis is necessary given scarcity.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the significance of the concept of scarcity and how it influences economic choices and decisions of various economic stakeholders.
cards.commonMisconception: Student thinks cost-benefit analysis is optional or only for businesses.

cards.question: A government has a limited budget and must choose between building a new hospital or a new highway. Identify one trade-off the government faces and state the opportunity cost if they choose the hospital.
cards.diagnosis: Assess higher-order understanding of trade-off and opportunity cost together.
cards.successCriteria: Student can identify trade-offs in a government decision and state the opportunity cost.
cards.ossdExpectation: Explain how the concepts of scarcity and opportunity costs influence economic decisions, at both the personal and societal levels.
cards.commonMisconception: Student lists consequences rather than alternatives when describing trade-offs.
